_comment: Mutations for the MCP surface: the scope gate, the auth resolver, the result framing and the 23 tools. Scored against mcp_run.sh, which is the only harness that speaks JSON-RPC, plus unit_run.sh for the pure functions. Two classes of mutation here are worth naming. First, the FRAMING ones: `structuredContent` is what a client parses mechanically, and every one of these mutations leaves a response that still reads correctly to a human. Second, the SCOPE ones: the gate is the whole of what a scoped key buys, and a mutation that widens it produces no error anywhere — the tool simply works for a key that should not have reached it. Each mutation carries its own DIFF_ONLY: the full run is 143 cases at two reseeds apiece and most of them cannot reach any given mutation. Narrowing can only remove cases, so it can only cost a catch. Three mutations are marked `_unit_only` — nothing a differential can drive reaches them, and the note on each says what does.

mutations.name: a readonly key gets every tool
mutations._why: The whole of what `readonly` buys. Widened, a key an operator minted to let an agent LOOK can also open incidents and change recording policy.

mutations.name: an empty custom scope means full access
mutations._why: `if not scope_tools` — absent OR empty is NO access. Falling through to `all_tools()` is the classic inverted default: the key with the narrowest configuration gets the widest reach.

mutations.name: a custom scope is not intersected with the catalog
mutations._why: Python intersects with MCP_ALL_TOOLS so an unknown name is dropped. Without it, a typo in a stored scope list becomes a name that matches nothing — harmless — but a LATER server-side write tool named by that typo would be silently enabled on an existing key. The leaked tool has to be one the fixture key does NOT already name: the first version of this mutation leaked `list_cameras`, which that key already has, and so behaved identically and scored zero.

mutations.name: the agent allowlist becomes a denylist
mutations._why: This is the security property the list exists for, stated in its own doc comment: the agent's model is steered by whatever an attacker can put in front of a lens, so a write tool has to be named IN rather than merely not named out. Inverted, every future write tool is enabled for the agent by default.

mutations.name: pro gets pro-plus rate limits
mutations._why: 30/min × 5000/day versus 120 × 30000. The tiers are four and six times apart, and a Pro key on Pro Plus limits is the paid difference given away.
mutations._unit_only: No case can spend 30 calls in a minute, so the differential cannot see this — `scope.rs`'s own tests and `mcp_parity.py` are what hold the numbers.

mutations.name: an arg summary is not shortened
mutations._why: 30 characters, cut to 27 plus an ellipsis. The summary goes in an audit row; a 64 kB `report` argument written whole turns the activity log into the storage for the report.
mutations._unit_only: The summary lands in `mcp_activity_logs` and in the tracker's ring, neither of which the MCP differential reads; the tracker's contents cannot be compared across a mutation run at all, because the runner restarts only the Rust tier and Python's ring survives. `scope.rs`'s own test is what holds it.

mutations.name: an integration key authenticates on the MCP surface
mutations._why: `kind='mcp'` on every McpApiKey query is what keeps the two key kinds from crossing surfaces. Dropped, an `osi_` key minted for Home Assistant — a key with NO scope picker and no tool gate — reaches all 23 tools.

mutations.name: a revoked key still works
mutations._why: Revocation is the only way to withdraw a key that has leaked. If the filter goes, the dashboard shows it revoked and it keeps working — the worst shape this bug can take. Scored zero until the fixture gained a real-hash revoked MCP key: the only revoked row with a hash a request could present was an INTEGRATION key, so the filter had nothing to act on and removing it changed nothing.

mutations.name: a list result is not wrapped
mutations._why: MCP requires an output schema to be an object, so FastMCP wraps a non-object return under `result` — and a client reading `structuredContent` mechanically gets an array where it expected `{result: [...]}`. Nothing about the response LOOKS wrong.

mutations.name: every result is wrapped
mutations._why: The other direction, which is the easier mistake: wrapping is a property of the tool's declared return type, not of the value, so a dict-returning tool must stay unwrapped.

mutations.name: an empty list still gets a text block
mutations._why: FastMCP checks whether every item is already a content block before serialising, and `all()` of nothing is true — so an empty list passes through as an empty block list. A `[]` text block is the plausible-looking wrong answer.

mutations.name: a write tool declares readOnlyHint false
mutations._why: Python decorates only the READ tools, so a write tool carries no annotations object at all. `readOnlyHint: false` says the same thing to a human reader and a different thing on the wire — present-and-false versus absent.

mutations.name: a read tool claims to be a write
mutations._why: The hint is what a client uses to decide whether a tool is safe to call speculatively. Inverted, a read tool needs confirmation and a write tool does not.

mutations.name: the derived title is the raw name
mutations._why: FastMCP always emits a title because some clients DROP a tool that has none rather than falling back to the name as the spec says. The underscored name is what a client would then show a user.

mutations.name: an error carries a structured half
mutations._why: FastMCP omits `structuredContent` entirely on an error. A client that branches on its presence would read a refusal as a result.

env.DIFF_ONLY: not found|an unknown tool|a revoked key

mutations.name: list_incidents swap-removes the report key
mutations._why: This one shipped. serde_json's `remove` is a SWAP-remove under `preserve_order`, so dropping `report` moves the LAST key into its slot — `evidence_count` lands between `summary` and `severity`. Every value is right and the key order is not.

mutations.name: an empty camera filter matches nothing
mutations._why: `if camera_id:` in get_stream_logs, `is not None` in list_incidents — the same argument name, the opposite answer for the empty string. Making them agree is a one-character change and it silently empties one of the two.
mutations.old:
let camera_id = opt_str(args, "camera_id").filter(|c| !c.is_empty());
    let limit = int_or(args, "limit", 50);
mutations.new:
let camera_id = opt_str(args, "camera_id");
    let limit = int_or(args, "limit", 50);

mutations.name: an empty camera_id is stored as NULL
mutations._why: Python's `if camera_id:` guards the existence check and nothing else — the column is assigned the argument as given. Normalising to NULL is the tidier-looking wrong answer, and it changes what the incident row says about which camera saw it.
mutations.old:
// is assigned the argument as given, so `""` is stored as `""`.
    .bind(&camera_id)
mutations.new:
// is assigned the argument as given, so `""` is stored as `""`.
    .bind(camera_id.as_deref().filter(|c| !c.is_empty()))

mutations.name: an empty note is stored as the empty string
mutations._why: `note.strip() if note else None` tests the UNSTRIPPED value, so `""` is NULL and `"   "` is `""`. Both read as “no caption” to a human and they are different rows — one has evidence text, one does not. Caught twice over: by the node-backed attach_snapshot cases, and by `python_note`'s own test — the second one because the first depends on a live socket and could age out.

mutations.name: has_data is read off the blob
mutations._why: `has_data` is `data_mime is not None`, which is NOT the same as “has bytes”: the fixture's evidence 16 has a blob and no MIME, and Python reports has_data FALSE for it. Reading the blob would also defeat the column's deferral, which is the reason the flag is derived this way at all.

mutations.name: a clip is truncated from the newest end
mutations._why: The cap drops the OLDEST segments: an agent asking for a clip wants the most recent video. Dropping from the other end returns the beginning of the buffer and reports the same duration for it. No differential case can reach this — the real cap is 32 MB, so triggering it would mean pushing tens of megabytes into each tier's segment cache per case, which is why `trim_to_cap` was extracted as a function and is tested against a ten-byte cap.
mutations._unit_only: 32 MB is out of a differential's reach; `trim_to_cap`'s own tests are what hold which end is dropped.

mutations.name: the incident daily cap is off by one
mutations._why: `>=`, so the 200th is the last one allowed. A `>` lets 201 through — which matters not for the extra row but because this cap is the rail against a prompt-injected loop, and an off-by-one here is the shape a real regression takes.
mutations._unit_only: Reaching it through the differential needs a fixture carrying 200 incidents in one day. An earlier version of this note claimed `tools.rs` already exercised the comparison; it did not, and the mutation scored zero. `daily_cap_refusal` was extracted so there is something to test, and `the_daily_cap_refuses_at_the_limit_not_past_it` is what catches this now.

mutations.name: a title is truncated by bytes
mutations._why: `title.strip()[:200]` counts CHARACTERS. Slicing bytes cuts a multi-byte character in half at the boundary — and the column is 200 characters wide, so a byte slice can still overflow it. Every title case in the differential was ASCII until this mutation scored zero, where bytes and characters agree; there are now a two-byte and an astral case as well.
mutations.new: let stored_title: String = title.trim().bytes().take(200).map(|b| b as char).collect();

mutations.name: both recording modes can be true at once
mutations._why: Continuous and scheduled are mutually exclusive, and the refusal is a RESULT rather than an error — a shape easy to drop entirely when porting, because nothing else in this file answers that way. Without it the camera gets a policy the dashboard cannot express. No case reached it until this mutation scored zero: each of the others set a mode whose counterpart was already off, so the conflict branch never ran.

mutations.name: an incident is found across orgs
mutations._why: The org filter on the ownership lookup is the tenant boundary for every incident write: observations, snapshots, clips, the report body. Without it an agent key for one org can append evidence to another's incident, and the response looks entirely normal. Reached by the two evidence readers' other-org cases (incident 4, evidence 4): with the filter gone they find another tenant's incident and return its evidence.

mutations.name: a revoked key is still scoped
mutations._why: The scope lookup runs on tools/list as well as tools/call, and it has its OWN copy of the kind+revoked filter. Only the call path is covered by the resolver's mutations above; this one is the catalog. Scored zero until the fixture gained a real-hash revoked MCP key: the only revoked row with a hash a request could present was an INTEGRATION key, so the filter had nothing to act on and removing it changed nothing.
